svg.title: How a MEMS gyro feels turning
svg.desc: Animated top view of the sensing part inside a MEMS gyro chip, drawn huge and simplified. A small blue mass hangs on springs inside a frame and vibrates left and right all the time. The gray platform carrying the chip sits still, turns a quarter turn left, waits, then turns back right. Only while it turns, the mass is also pushed sideways, across its vibration (the Coriolis effect), one way for a left turn and the other way for a right turn. A turn-rate bar on the right fills only while the platform turns, and a heading needle and number change only while it turns, because heading is the turn rate added up over time. Notes: a vibrating mass gets pushed sideways when the chip turns (the Coriolis effect), and that push is the turn rate. Heading is the rate added up, so any tiny error adds up too: drift. Redux Canandgyro: calibrate it still for at least 7 s; drift about 0.2 deg an hour still, 0.25 deg a minute moving.
svg.text: How a MEMS gyro feels turning
Top view of the sensing part inside the chip, drawn huge and simplified.
Turning: the mass also wiggles sideways

g.text: Turning, the Coriolis effect pushes the swinging mass sideways,
back and forth with each swing: how far says how fast it turns.
Heading is the rate added up, so any tiny error adds up too: drift.
Redux Canandgyro: calibrate it still for at least 7 s; drift about
0.2 deg an hour still, 0.25 deg a minute moving.
